conventions: Each probe has a unique id (P01...). distractor_set items are {option, trap}; trap is a trap ID or "partial". A probe listed under one trap may also offer co-traps; the trap named on each distractor is the one choosing it diagnoses. flag:"unverified" means the key or its refutation rests on an unverified claim: place it only in an exam-trap or deeper node, shown with the warning sign. Feedback must say only what the cited claims say.

traps.trap: ASD, PDA or LVH is part of the four classic components of TOF (or a true component is picked as the 'NOT' answer)

probes.stem_idea: Which of the following is NOT a component of classic tetralogy of Fallot?
probes.note: Surfaces TR1 early. 'Infundibular stenosis' catches the valve-only model (TR2 holder thinks 'infundibular' is wrong); 'RVH' catches the left-sided store (TR14 holder expects LVH). Feedback cites K3, K13, K77 and teaches the PYQ key: ASD/PDA/LVH are 'not part of TOF'.

probes.stem_idea: Echo of a cyanotic 6-month-old: anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, sub-pulmonary narrowing, thick RV wall and a small ASD. Which finding is an accompanying lesion rather than one of the four?
probes.note: Same idea, echo-report surface. Choosing 'thick RV wall' = thinks RVH is not part of the defect set because it is acquired (TR2 confusion of primary vs secondary). Cite K13 (ASD and PDA may accompany TOF), K3, K12.

probes.stem_idea: Which set lists the four components of classic TOF?
probes.correct: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH

distractor_set.option: VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, ASD
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, LVH

probes.note: Re-test in the exam-traps or consolidate segment. Lengths matched as four-item lists. The third option is the 'extra shunts' model that also feeds pentalogy confusion (TR3).

traps.diagnoses: The learner stores TOF as a list of familiar shunt lesions rather than as one anteriorly malaligned septum with its consequences, so any common shunt (ASD, PDA) or any 'ventricular hypertrophy' slips into the list.

repair.strategy: E2: rebuild the four from their logic. One anteriorly malaligned VSD lets the aorta override and narrows the infundibulum; the RV then hypertrophies (secondary). ASD and PDA are lesions that may accompany TOF, not members of the set. Close with a 'which is NOT' re-test. Teach both: PYQs keyed ASD/PDA/LVH as 'not part of TOF'; StatPearls lists the four.

traps.retest: P01 (which-is-not) surfaces it in the core-anatomy segment; P02 (vignette) in clinical diagnosis; P03 (recognition of the full set) in exam traps or consolidate. Also offered on P05 and P07.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know the four as one malformation, not a list. Fell and recovered: you first added a familiar shunt, then rebuilt the four from the malaligned septum; keep deriving them, not memorising them. Fell repeatedly: you are treating TOF as a list of shunts; redraw the anatomy from the malaligned VSD and run 'which is NOT' questions until ASD/PDA/LVH stand out.

traps.trap: The RVOT obstruction is purely valvular, and RVH is a primary defect (or the cause) rather than a consequence

probes.stem_idea: In classic TOF, the right ventricular outflow obstruction lies chiefly at which level?
probes.note: Predict-then-show. Cite K11 and K3. Avoid claiming the valve is always normal; the bank only says infundibular.

probes.stem_idea: Of the four components, which one develops as a consequence of the others rather than as a primary malformation?
probes.note: Choosing infundibular obstruction = believes the thick RV causes the narrowing (cause and effect reversed). Choosing overriding aorta = has no causal model of the set at all, just a list (TR1). Cite K12 ('secondary to chronic systemic pressures').

traps.diagnoses: The learner has the right words but the wrong causal chain: they think the obstruction is a simple valve stenosis and that the hypertrophied RV is a primary defect, so they cannot reason forward to the ECG, X-ray or spell physiology.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show. Ask what happens to a ventricle pumping against an obstructed outflow at systemic pressure, then show K12: RVH is secondary. Trace the chain step by step: malaligned septum, infundibular narrowing, RV pressure load, RVH.

traps.retest: P04 (mechanism) in core anatomy; P05 (sequence) later in the same segment or in consolidate. Also offered on P01 and P02.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know the obstruction is infundibular and RVH is secondary. Fell and recovered: you first reversed cause and effect, then traced the chain; keep starting from the outflow obstruction. Fell repeatedly: you treat RVH as a primary defect; trace septum to infundibulum to RV pressure to RVH before answering anatomy stems.

traps.trap: Pentalogy of Fallot adds something other than an ASD (PDA, a second VSD)

probes.stem_idea: Pentalogy of Fallot is tetralogy of Fallot plus:
probes.note: Cite K5 and K76; mention the term is old and seldom used now.

probes.stem_idea: Which statement about TOF and an accompanying ASD is correct?
probes.correct: An ASD may accompany TOF; TOF plus ASD is the old 'pentalogy'

distractor_set.option: An ASD is one of the four classic components of TOF
Pentalogy is TOF plus a PDA; an ASD plays no part

probes.note: Places TR1 and TR3 side by side so the learner sees the ASD sits outside the four but inside the pentalogy. Cite K13, K5, K76.

traps.diagnoses: The learner treats ASD and PDA as interchangeable 'extra shunts', so the fifth member of the pentalogy is a guess between them.

repair.strategy: E2: rebuild the set: four from the malaligned septum, plus an ASD makes five. Contrast ASD (pentalogy) with PDA (may accompany, not the fifth). Re-test with a contrast stem.

traps.retest: P06 (recognition) right after the four components are rebuilt; P07 (contrast) in exam traps. Also offered on P03.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know pentalogy is TOF plus ASD. Fell and recovered: you first swapped in a PDA, then fixed the fifth component. Fell repeatedly: you are treating ASD and PDA as interchangeable; anchor 'pentalogy = TOF + ASD' to the old CDC term and keep PDA as a lesion that may accompany.

traps.trap: The boot-shaped heart is always or usually present in TOF, or is caused by the LV or a large pulmonary artery

probes.stem_idea: The upturned apex of the 'boot-shaped' heart in TOF is due to:
probes.note: Cite K4, K32 (upturned apex from RVH with a concave pulmonary arterial segment). The 'dilated PA' option is the reverse of the concave segment.

probes.stem_idea: A 3-month-old with echo-confirmed TOF has a chest X-ray without a boot-shaped heart. How do you read this?
probes.correct: It does not exclude TOF; the boot shape is a 'may classically' sign

distractor_set.option: It argues against TOF; the boot shape is always present
It suggests the lung fields will look plethoric instead

probes.note: Counter-case re-test for the superlative. Core claim K4 ('may classically') is verified; Radiopaedia's 'most infants may not show this finding' (K78/K33) is unverified, so place this probe in the exam-traps node with the warning sign and teach both: PYQs keyed boot-shaped heart to TOF; Radiopaedia says most infants may not show it.

traps.diagnoses: The learner has turned 'boot-shaped heart = TOF' into an always-present sign and has lost its mechanism, so they misread a normal film or attribute the apex to the wrong chamber.

repair.strategy: E4: show the exact qualifier ('may classically show', K4) and a counter-case (an echo-confirmed infant without the boot). Pair with the mechanism: RVH lifts the apex, the pulmonary arterial segment is concave, lungs are oligaemic.

traps.retest: P08 (mechanism) in the investigations segment; P09 (vignette counter-case, warning-flagged) in exam traps. Also offered on P13 (diagnostic test vignette).
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know the boot shape is a classic sign with a right-sided cause, not a must-have. Fell and recovered: you first stretched 'classic' into 'always' or blamed the LV, then corrected it. Fell repeatedly: you are treating a 'may classically' sign as universal; read the qualifier and name the chamber (RV) every time.

traps.trap: Confusing the TOF radiograph with other cyanotic CHD signs, or expecting increased pulmonary vascularity

probes.stem_idea: A boot-shaped heart on chest X-ray is classically seen in:
probes.note: PYQ form (AIIMS 2019 recall). Feedback refutes via K4 only; the bank has no verified claim on the TGA or TAPVR films (Unrefutable list), so do not state which sign belongs to them.

probes.stem_idea: Which chest X-ray description fits TOF?
probes.correct: Normal-sized heart, upturned apex, oligaemic lung fields

distractor_set.option: Egg-on-a-string heart with a narrow pedicle

probes.note: Re-test with a description surface. Cite K31 and K21. Again, do not assign egg-on-a-string to another lesion as a fact.

traps.diagnoses: The learner has memorised the cyanotic CHD radiograph signs as one undifferentiated list and pairs them by guesswork rather than by the TOF mechanism (RV apex, concave PA segment, oligaemia).

repair.strategy: E10: pair recall anchored to mechanism. Build the TOF film from the physiology (K31, K21, K32) so that 'boot' plus 'oligaemia' belongs to TOF; contrast with the other descriptions only by what the TOF film is not.

traps.retest: P10 (recognition, PYQ form) in exam traps; P11 (contrast of descriptions) in the investigations segment or consolidate.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you pair the boot-shaped, oligaemic film with TOF. Fell and recovered: you first mixed the cyanotic CHD signs, then anchored the TOF film to its mechanism. Fell repeatedly: you are matching signs from a list; derive the TOF film from RVH and low pulmonary flow before matching.

traps.trap: 'Most common cyanotic CHD' with the age qualifier dropped or reversed

probes.stem_idea: The most common cyanotic congenital heart disease is:
probes.note: Hook or retrieve segment; verified claims K1, K69. Two buttons is acceptable here; do not add filler options. Feedback must not state that TGA is the commonest in neonates (Unrefutable list); say only that the unqualified stem keys TOF.

probes.stem_idea: Two lines: a PYQ says 'most common cyanotic CHD beyond the neonatal period'; StatPearls says TOF 'most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate'. Which answer is safe in the exam?
probes.correct: TOF is the most common cyanotic CHD; PYQs add 'beyond the neonatal period'

distractor_set.option: TOF is the most common cyanotic CHD specifically in the neonate
TOF is never cyanotic until after the neonatal period ends

probes.note: Teach both (K75, K2, K70 unverified; K1, K24 verified). Exam-traps node with the warning sign.

traps.diagnoses: The learner carries 'most common cyanotic CHD' without its qualifier, so they cannot tell an unqualified stem from an age-qualified one and conflate 'presents as a cyanotic neonate' with 'commonest in neonates'.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier and contrast the two settings. Unqualified: TOF (K1). PYQs expected 'beyond the neonatal period' (K2/K70, unverified); StatPearls says TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate (K24). Presentation age and 'most common' are different statements.

traps.retest: P12 (recognition) in the hook/retrieve segment; P12b (contrast, warning-flagged) in exam traps.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you read the age qualifier before answering 'most common'. Fell and recovered: you first dropped the qualifier, then separated 'commonest' from 'presents as'. Fell repeatedly: you answer superlatives without the qualifier; underline the age group in every 'most common' stem.

traps.trap: Every TOF is cyanotic from birth; acyanotic 'pink Tets' are missed

probes.stem_idea: A 2-month-old, not diagnosed before birth, is pink and feeding well with a loud harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border; echo shows TOF. Best explanation?
probes.correct: Moderate RVOT obstruction, so he is a 'pink Tet'

distractor_set.option: The echo is wrong; TOF is always cyanotic at birth
The murmur is loud because he is in a spell

probes.note: Cite K23, K25. The spell option pre-surfaces TR8 before it is taught.

probes.stem_idea: A child with TOF is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic when:
probes.correct: RVOT resistance is less than systemic vascular resistance

distractor_set.option: Never; every TOF is cyanotic from birth
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises above normal

probes.note: Cite K22. This is the backbone 'RVOT vs SVR' balance that TR8-TR11 build on, so place it just before the spell segment.

traps.diagnoses: The learner equates 'cyanotic heart disease' with 'blue at birth' and has no model of cyanosis as a balance between RVOT and systemic resistance.

repair.strategy: E4: show the exact qualifier and a counter-case: StatPearls says TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate (K24), and also describes pink Tets with only a loud murmur (K23). Then the balance rule (K22).

traps.retest: P14 (vignette) in the clinical-picture segment; P15 (mechanism) at the start of the spell segment. Also offered on P12b.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know cyanosis in TOF depends on RVOT versus systemic resistance. Fell and recovered: you first assumed every TOF is blue, then met the pink Tet. Fell repeatedly: you are stretching 'most commonly cyanotic' into 'always'; recall the pink Tet with only a loud murmur.

traps.trap: During a tet spell the murmur gets louder

probes.stem_idea: Predict: during a hypercyanotic spell, the systolic murmur of TOF:
probes.note: Ask confidence; a confident 'louder' gets a sure_note. Then show K29 and explain via K20: with severe obstruction blood bypasses the pulmonary bed, so less crosses the RVOT. Contrast with K26 (more obstruction, more prominent murmur) to show why the intuition is tempting.

probes.stem_idea: A 4-month-old with known TOF is crying, deeply cyanosed and breathing fast; the murmur heard last week is now hard to hear. What is happening?

distractor_set.option: Heart failure from left ventricular dysfunction

probes.note: Re-test on a clinical surface. Cite K29, K28 (triggers include agitation).

traps.diagnoses: The learner applies the general rule 'worse stenosis, louder murmur' to a dynamic spell, so they read a softening murmur as improvement instead of falling RVOT flow.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show. Trace the spell: RVOT flow falls, more blood shunts to the aorta, so the RVOT murmur softens (K29, K20). Contrast with the baseline rule (K26).

traps.retest: P16 (mechanism, predict) opens the spell segment; P17 (vignette) re-tests it in the management case. Also offered on P14 and P29.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know the murmur softens in a spell. Fell and recovered: you first expected a louder murmur, then traced the falling RVOT flow. Fell repeatedly: you are applying 'worse obstruction, louder murmur' to a spell; ask how much blood is crossing the RVOT right now.

traps.trap: Knee-chest position (squatting) works by lowering PVR or raising pulmonary flow directly, not by raising systemic vascular resistance

probes.stem_idea: Knee-chest positioning helps a child in a tet spell by:

distractor_set.option: Reducing venous return to the right heart

probes.note: Cite K43. Squatting has no claim in the bank (Unrefutable list); if the dialogue mentions the squatting PYQ (AIIMS 2017), keep it as a stem cue and teach only the knee-chest mechanism the claim supports.

probes.stem_idea: Which two tet-spell measures share the same aim of raising systemic afterload?
probes.note: Contrast SVR (K43, K47) with pulmonary vasodilation by oxygen (K44): someone who believes positioning acts on the lungs pairs it with oxygen.

traps.diagnoses: The learner knows positioning improves lung flow but misplaces the lever: they think it acts on pulmonary resistance instead of raising systemic resistance so that less blood shunts right-to-left.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show using the K22 balance: if systemic resistance rises above RVOT resistance, blood is pushed to the lungs. Positioning and phenylephrine raise SVR (K43, K47); oxygen acts on the pulmonary side (K44).

traps.retest: P18 (mechanism) in the spell segment; P19 (contrast) in management or exam traps. Also offered on P15, P22 and P23.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know positioning raises systemic vascular resistance. Fell and recovered: you first swapped PVR for SVR, then rebuilt the balance. Fell repeatedly: you are mixing up PVR and SVR; for every spell measure ask which side of the shunt it pushes on.

traps.trap: Tet spell management starts with drugs or intubation; positioning and oxygen are skipped

probes.stem_idea: A 6-month-old with TOF goes into a tet spell in the OPD. What do you do first?
probes.note: Ask confidence. Order follows the StatPearls list (K43 first, then K44, K45, K46, K47, K48); the verifier should check the dialogue claims no more priority than that list supports. K42: rapid, aggressive approach.

probes.stem_idea: Put the tet-spell steps in order.
probes.correct: Knee-chest and oxygen, then IV fluids, then beta-blocker or phenylephrine

distractor_set.option: Phenylephrine, then morphine, then knee-chest and oxygen
Oxygen, then IV furosemide, then digoxin

probes.note: Re-test as an ordering task in consolidate. Lengths roughly matched.

traps.diagnoses: The learner knows the list of spell treatments but not their order, and reaches for the most 'active' drug before the simple bedside measures.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps and ask 'what first, and why'. Bedside first (knee-chest, oxygen), then volume, then drugs that slow the heart or raise afterload, with morphine as a sedative.

traps.retest: P20 (first step in a case) in the management segment; P21 (ordering) in consolidate.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you start a spell with position and oxygen. Fell and recovered: you first reached for a drug, then put the bedside steps first. Fell repeatedly: you know the treatments but not the order; rehearse knee-chest and oxygen, fluids, then drugs.

traps.trap: Spells are treated like heart failure (inotrope, diuretic, fluid restriction) or by lowering afterload

probes.stem_idea: Why are IV fluid boluses given in a tet spell?

distractor_set.option: They are avoided; fluid worsens failure

probes.note: Cite K45; link to K46 (beta-blockers slow the rate and aid RV filling).

probes.stem_idea: Which of these is NOT part of tet-spell treatment?
probes.note: The bank lists the treatments (K43-K48) and their aims; no claim names furosemide, so feedback refutes it by aim (raise SVR, fill the RV) rather than by a direct 'contraindicated' statement. Choosing phenylephrine = thinks raising afterload is harmful (TR9 lever reversed).

traps.diagnoses: The learner brings heart-failure reflexes (diuretic, inotrope, restrict fluid) to a dynamic outflow spasm, so they act against filling the RV and raising systemic afterload.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show. Trace what each measure does to RV filling and systemic afterload: fluids fill the RV (K45), beta-blockers slow the rate and aid filling (K46), phenylephrine raises afterload (K47), oxygen dilates the pulmonary bed (K44).

traps.retest: P22 (mechanism) in the management case; P23 (which-is-not) in exam traps. Also offered on P17, P18, P19, P20, P21.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you treat a spell by filling the RV and raising afterload. Fell and recovered: you first reached for heart-failure measures, then traced RV filling. Fell repeatedly: you are treating a spell like heart failure; ask what each drug does to RV filling and systemic resistance.

traps.trap: Catheterisation, CT or MRI is the gold standard for diagnosing TOF

probes.stem_idea: The gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of TOF is:
probes.note: Cite K6, K34, K72.

probes.stem_idea: A cyanotic 2-month-old has a harsh ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border and right axis deviation on ECG. Which test confirms the diagnosis?

distractor_set.option: Chest X-ray for a boot-shaped heart

probes.note: Re-test on a clinical surface. Choosing the X-ray = treats a 'may classically' sign as confirmatory (TR4). Cite K35, K4.

traps.diagnoses: The learner ranks tests by invasiveness or detail rather than by the question asked, so a historical or adjunct test displaces echo as the diagnostic standard.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers: echo diagnoses (gold standard, K6, K34, K35); CT shows complex morphology (K37); MRI adds anatomy and function without radiation (K39).

traps.retest: P24 (recognition) in investigations; P13 (vignette) in the clinical case or exam traps. Also offered on P25 and P26.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you name echo as the diagnostic gold standard. Fell and recovered: you first chose a more invasive test, then placed each on the ladder. Fell repeatedly: you pick tests by detail, not by the question; ask 'diagnose, or plan surgery?'.

traps.trap: Echo, CT and MRI are interchangeable; echo needs no adjunct, or MRI is first-line

probes.stem_idea: Echo has confirmed TOF; before repair the team wants the complex cardiovascular morphology shown in detail. Which test adds this?
probes.note: Cite K37 (verified). K36 and K40 (echo limits for peripheral PS; why PA assessment matters) are unverified: use only in a deeper branch with the warning sign.

probes.stem_idea: Which pairing of test and job is right in TOF?
probes.correct: Echo for diagnosis; MRI for anatomy plus function without radiation

distractor_set.option: MRI for first-line diagnosis; echo for follow-up only
Catheterisation for diagnosis; echo for screening only

probes.note: Cite K35, K39, K6.

traps.diagnoses: The learner treats imaging tests as interchangeable, so they either stop at echo when surgical anatomy is needed or promote MRI to first-line diagnosis.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers, as for TR12, with the surgical-planning rung added (CT morphology, MRI anatomy and function).

traps.retest: P25 (vignette) in investigations or a deeper branch; P26 (contrast) in exam traps or consolidate. Also offered on P24.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know what each imaging test adds. Fell and recovered: you first treated the tests as interchangeable, then matched each to its job. Fell repeatedly: map each test to one question: diagnose, show morphology, add function.

traps.trap: ECG and chest X-ray in TOF show left-sided changes (LVH, left axis, plethora, cardiomegaly)

probes.stem_idea: The ECG in TOF typically shows:
probes.correct: Right axis deviation with RVH pattern

distractor_set.option: Left axis deviation with LVH pattern

probes.note: Cite K30 (right axis deviation, prominent R/qR in V1, upright T in V1, RAE and RVH).

probes.stem_idea: Predict the lung fields on a TOF chest X-ray from where the blood goes.
probes.correct: Oligaemic: blood bypasses the pulmonary bed

distractor_set.option: Plethoric: the VSD floods the lungs

probes.note: Cite K20, K21, K31 (normal-size heart silhouette). Predict-then-show re-test of the left-sided / plethoric model on a different surface.

traps.diagnoses: The learner stored 'ventricular hypertrophy' without its side and assumes shunt lesions make the lungs plethoric, so the right-sided, oligaemic picture of TOF is reversed.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show from the chain built for TR2: RV pressure load gives RVH, so right axis and tall R in V1 (K30, K12); flow bypasses the lungs, so oligaemia and a normal-sized heart (K20, K21, K31).

traps.retest: Surfaced early on P01 and P04; P27 (ECG recognition) and P30 (lung-field mechanism) in investigations; re-tested on P08, P09, P11 and P03 in exam traps or consolidate.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you keep the TOF ECG and film right-sided and oligaemic. Fell and recovered: you first put the changes on the left, then derived them from the RV load. Fell repeatedly: you are storing 'hypertrophy' without a side; derive it from which ventricle faces the obstruction.

traps.trap: P2 is loud or S2 widely split in TOF

probes.stem_idea: In TOF, the pulmonary component of S2 is usually:
probes.note: Cite K27. Do not state facts about pulmonary hypertension or ASD auscultation; the bank has none.

probes.stem_idea: Which auscultatory finding does NOT fit TOF?
probes.correct: A loud pulmonary component of S2

distractor_set.option: An inaudible pulmonary component of S2
A murmur that softens during a spell

probes.note: A learner holding the loud-P2 model rejects 'inaudible P2' as not fitting. Cite K27, K25, K29.

traps.diagnoses: The learner links 'pulmonary' lesions with a loud P2, borrowing the sound of a high-pressure pulmonary circuit for a lesion where little blood reaches the pulmonary valve.

repair.strategy: E1: contrasting cases: put the TOF auscultation (harsh ejection murmur at the left mid-upper sternal border, inaudible P2) beside the loud-P2 idea and name the discriminating feature: low flow across the pulmonary side.

traps.retest: P28 (recognition) in the clinical-picture segment; P29 (which-is-not) in exam traps.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you expect an inaudible P2 in TOF. Fell and recovered: you first borrowed a loud P2, then linked P2 to low pulmonary flow. Fell repeatedly: you are importing a loud P2 from other lesions; ask how much blood reaches the pulmonary valve.

traps.trap: Down syndrome (or another syndrome) is the usual TOF association, or 22q11.2 deletion is in most cases

probes.stem_idea: The most common syndromic association of TOF is:
probes.note: K7 and K71 are unverified: exam-traps node with the warning sign. Do not state the Down-AVSD link as a fact; the bank has no claim for it.

probes.stem_idea: Roughly what share of TOF carries a 22q11.2 deletion?
probes.note: K79 (verified) states the sources differ, 15% vs 6%; K17 and K18 are unverified. Teach both figures.

traps.diagnoses: The learner pairs the best-known CHD syndrome with TOF by familiarity, and inflates 'most common association' into 'present in most cases'.

repair.strategy: E10: pair recall: 22q11.2 deletion with TOF; contrast the size of the share (up to 15% vs 6%) with 'most cases'. Shown with the warning sign because the association claims are unverified.

traps.retest: P31 (recognition) and P32 (numbers) both in exam traps or a deeper branch, separated by at least one other probe.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you pair TOF with 22q11.2 deletion and keep its share modest. Fell and recovered: you first reached for Down syndrome or an inflated share, then corrected it. Fell repeatedly: you are matching syndromes by fame; anchor TOF to 22q11.2 and remember 'most common' is not 'most cases'.

traps.trap: Incidence figures and right aortic arch frequency confused

probes.stem_idea: A right aortic arch is seen in about what proportion of TOF?
probes.note: Cite K19. Anchor: roughly one in four or five.

probes.stem_idea: Two sources quote TOF incidence. Which pairing is right?
probes.correct: StatPearls 5–7 and Garagiola 3–5 per 10,000 live births

distractor_set.option: StatPearls 3–5 and Garagiola 5–7 per 10,000 live births
Both quote about 1 in 300 live births

probes.note: K80 (verified) carries the spread; K15 and K16 are unverified, so keep this in a deeper branch or exam-traps node with the warning sign if K15 is quoted on its own.

traps.diagnoses: The learner holds the numbers loosely, without an anchor, so similar-sounding figures from different sources swap places.

repair.strategy: E6: anchor each number to something meaningful (right arch about one in four or five; incidence a few per 10,000, with sources disagreeing) and re-test in a different form.

traps.retest: P33 (numbers) in a deeper branch on associations; P34 (contrast) in exam traps.
traps.report_hint: Avoided: your TOF numbers are anchored. Fell and recovered: you first swapped figures, then anchored them. Fell repeatedly: tie each figure to an anchor rather than memorising digits; these are low-yield, so do not over-invest.

traps.trap: Complete repair is neonatal for all, or delayed to school age; a BT shunt is the routine first step

probes.stem_idea: A well, asymptomatic 6-week-old with TOF and good-sized pulmonary arteries. When is complete repair usually planned?
probes.correct: Electively, after the first 3 months of life

distractor_set.option: BT shunt now, repair years later

probes.note: Core key rests on K50 (verified) and K49 (timing still debated). The 3–6 months window (K51) is unverified: mention only with the warning sign.

probes.stem_idea: Which TOF infant is the candidate for initial palliation before repair?
probes.correct: A premature, low-birth-weight infant with small pulmonary arteries

distractor_set.option: A thriving 4-month-old with good-sized pulmonary arteries

probes.note: K55 and K56 are unverified: deeper or exam-traps node with the warning sign.

traps.diagnoses: The learner applies one timeline to every infant and ignores the qualifiers (symptomatic or not, high-risk features) that decide timing and staging.

probes.correct: Subclavian artery to ipsilateral pulmonary artery

distractor_set.option: Ascending aorta to right pulmonary artery
Descending aorta to left pulmonary artery
Superior vena cava to right pulmonary artery

probes.note: Cite K54 (verified). The bank has no claim naming the Waterston, Potts or Glenn connections, so feedback must not assign those eponyms as facts.

probes.stem_idea: In the surgical plan for TOF, the Blalock-Taussig shunt is:
probes.correct: A palliative shunt, not the definitive repair

distractor_set.option: The definitive repair of the four defects
A routine first step for every TOF infant

probes.note: K53 and K57 (palliative; limited lifespan) are unverified: exam-traps node with the warning sign.

probes.note: Cite K61, K73; K59 for valve replacement routes.

probes.correct: It results from reconstruction of the RVOT

distractor_set.option: It results from reopening of the VSD patch
It results from left ventricular failure

traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know the repair's own legacy is pulmonary regurgitation. Fell and recovered: you first expected old defects to return, then traced the RVOT reconstruction. Fell repeatedly: ask what the operation itself changes, not which defect comes back.

probes.correct: Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death remain risks

Endocarditis risk ended with the repair

probe_plan: Three wrong models drive most traps. Backbone 1, 'TOF is a list of shunts with a left-sided picture' (TR1, with TR2, TR3, TR14, TR15 and the cause half of TR4): fix it first in the core-anatomy segment by rebuilding the four from one anteriorly malaligned septum (P01, P04, P05, P06), then let the ECG and film follow from RV load and low pulmonary flow (P27, P30, P08, P11), with P02 and P03 as later re-tests. Backbone 2, 'cyanosis is fixed by the anatomy' versus the RVOT-against-SVR balance (TR7, TR8, TR9, TR10, TR11): P15 (K22 balance) is the prerequisite and should open the spell segment, followed by P16 (murmur softens), P18 (knee-chest raises SVR), P20 (first step), P22 (fluids fill the RV); re-test with P14/P17 (vignettes), P19 (SVR contrast), P21 (ordering) and P23 (which-is-not). Backbone 3, superlatives and qualifiers stretched (TR6, TR4, TR7, TR18, TR20, TR21): meet TR6 in the hook (P12) and TR4 in investigations (P08) so both can be re-tested in exam traps (P12b, P09, both warning-flagged). Order: TR6 (hook) > TR1 > TR3 > TR2 > TR14 > TR15 > TR7 > TR4 > TR5 > TR12 > TR13 > TR8 > TR9 > TR10 > TR11 > TR18 > TR19 > TR20 > TR21 > TR22 > TR16 > TR17, with exam traps and consolidate carrying the second probes. Probes where competing traps sit in one stem: P01, P03, P07 (TR1/TR2/TR3/TR14 component and pentalogy set), P08, P09, P11 (TR4/TR5/TR14 radiograph), P18, P19, P20, P21, P22, P23 (TR9/TR10/TR11 spell management), P24, P25, P26 (TR12/TR13 test ladder), P38 (TR18/TR19 surgery), P29 (TR15/TR8 auscultation). Backbone traps: TR1, TR2, TR9, TR10, TR4, TR6. Warning-flagged probes (unverified keys or refutations) go only in exam-trap or deeper nodes: P09, P12b, P31, P32, P36, P38, and P34 if K15 is quoted alone. Low-yield traps (TR13, TR15, TR17, TR22) may sit in deeper branches. Design check: every trap has at least two probes in different forms; each distractor names one trap; no stem keys a fact from the Unrefutable list (TGA as neonatal commonest, egg-on-a-string, snowman, squatting mechanism, Waterston/Potts/Glenn and Down-AVSD links are never asserted in feedback); every high-yield trap is surfaced in segments 1-5 and re-tested later.
